newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Economists expect market friendly Swedish budget.
newsitem.headline: Economists expect market friendly Swedish budget.

text.p: The Swedish government is expected to confirm a slightly brighter-than-forecast picture when it hands down its 1997 budget on Friday with unemployment the only cloud on the horizon.

Economists were not expecting Finance Minister Erik Asbrink to pull any more surprises after outlining proposals to save 22 billion crowns ($3.3 billion) in 1997 and 1998 through spending cuts and tax increases in his debut budget in April this year.

They said, however, he could fill in some of the details left out in April and revise some of the government's economic forecasts after a stronger-than-expected performance in recent months -- although unemployment forecasts could be raised.

"The main message from the budget will be to point out that the situation is much better than a year ago and much better than people thought it would be six months ago," Aragon economist Tomas Niemela told Reuters.

Economists said public finances had improved markedly this year and Sweden will easily meet the Maastricht Treaty goal of a budget deficit of three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by 1997, the key year for deciding which countries qualify for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
In April the government forecast the budget deficit at 2.7 percent of GDP in 1997, but this could now be revised.

Economists said Sweden is headed for a balanced or even surplus budget in 1998 versus a deficit of 12.4 percent of GDP in 1993 with the 1996 public sector borrowing need now seen at 40-50 billion crowns versus April's 76 billion crowns forecast.
Economist Magnus Matsoms from Carnegie said the markets would be watching to see how the government had decided to carry out spending cuts announced earlier but not specified.
"If they specify these measures, revise the growth forecast upwards and the inflation outlook downwards, it could be a market friendly budget," Matsoms told Reuters.
"They don't need any new measures to meet earlier targets."
Economist Mikael Bostrom from S-E-Banken did not expect the budget to have much impact on the financial markets. Other economists suggested a neutral to slightly positive effect.
Rising unemployment remained a blot on the budget paper but Bostrom said this would be dealt with in a separate package.
"But it will be interesting, as always, to see how the government evaluates the pace of the monetary convergence proposals," Bostrom told Reuters.
"Another important thing is that this is the first budget based on a new budget system where specific ceilings for expenditure are set for a large number of areas."
The traditionally high-spending Nordic state has, for the first time, set expenditure ceilings for 27 separate areas in the public sector to keep tighter control over state finances.
Bostrom said the government could lift its growth forecast to 1.5 percent in 1996 from April's forecast of 1.4 percent and to 2.2 percent for 1997 against 2.0 percent five months ago.

Recent reports showing lower-than-expected inflation could prompt the government to lower April's 1996 forecast of 1.9 percent to just over 1.0 percent and for 1997 to between 1.5-2.0 percent from 2.3 percent in the spring budget.
Economists were mixed on whether the government would increase its forecasts for unemployment of 7.2 percent in 1996 and 6.5 percent in 1997.
But all were sceptical of Prime Minister Goran Persson's goal to halve unemployment to four percent by the year 2000.
"That target is looking a bit tentative," Niemela said.
With the budget not seen pulling any punches, Swedish newspapers, usually full of leaks, were low on forecasts.
Most papers forecast a two percent rise in tax on alcohol and a hike of between eight-nine percent on tobacco duty and a two percent rise in the energy tax on fuel, oil and petrol.
($1=6.633 Swedish Crown)
